sentences.text: Hi, Andy.
Oh, hi.
How are you doing?
I'm good, how are you?
Yeah, I'm good.
Sorry, Lisa, I was.
I was just making a coffee and I got back to my laptop and it died.
No problem.
Added up to five minute.
Five minutes late.
So apologies for that.
How is everything going in London today?
All good, yeah.
I'm at home today, but all good.
Obviously trying to work out what the budget all means for the business and personally and juggling all of that.
And we had our.
We had a big event at Meta that we hosted last week, which was exciting.
So that's been keeping the team busy.
So, yeah, lots going on at the end of the year.
God, that sounds exciting.
What.
What were you doing?
Was it an event?
Was it?
Yeah, we ran.
Well, we used to call it Kids Con, but now we just changed it to FAMF Fest and we ran it at Meta's offices on Euston Road.
We had about 150 people.
Yeah, it was really good.
The guys, all of our team presented and the material was really strong.
So we've had really strong feedback.
So, yes, good, good event.
But, yeah, it's definitely a lot of hard work on the run up to these things.
Yeah, brilliant.
Well, you'd be looking forward to the festive period then, no doubt.
Yeah.
How about you?
Andy for it.
Yeah, just so busy right now.
There's a few deals that have been ready to close the last two or three weeks and they just seem to be dragging on and on.
And these things, if they get into the second week of December, then it ends up being next year.
And next year is.
Is a graveyard for deals.
So I don't.
I don't want to get to next year.
If I could possibly close them this year, that'd be good thing.
Yeah.
Thank you for your.
Your time.
Appreciate your message to Katie.

I just wanted to go through it, kind of make sure that we were clear on it before I talked through because there was a couple of lines that were slightly ambiguous and I wasn't quite sure whether you are talking about an acquisition anymore or whether it seemed more like a partnership or what your thoughts were.
We're definitely looking for an acquisition, but I think an acquisition, slash, partnership.
So I think if we're bringing someone on and paying them the salary that she was quoting, I think we'd want them fully invested in the future and the growth of the business.
So I think we were looking at a part acquisition based on the numbers that you quoted with then a payout and an upside payout based on future performance.
So what would that look like?
A partial acquisition.
So would that be a minority or majority, but just not all of it?
I think we would want the.
I.
Think there's two ways of looking at it.

We had a board meeting yesterday and we were discussing it and we were talking about a longer term deal on it, which we were talking more like a five year deal on it, particularly with her aspirations.
If we were sponsoring her to come out over to the UK in year two or three, we would then want her building something out in the UK that she was leading.

So I think we, we would need probably a longer minimum term if we're going to guarantee on those elements because what we don't obviously want to do is bring her over to the UK and then, and then not do like we're paying her but not doing anything specifically in the PR arena because obviously currently we're, we're media only, we don't do anything on the PR side of things.

And then yeah, usually we, we would definitely want a majority stake in the business from the offset but we, to be honest, because we wanted to see whether that was even an option for her at this stage.
We haven't really gone into details of what a framework of a deal might look like.
I know just, just from.

I went to a more Kingston Smith event the other day and they were saying, I don't know if you're seeing this but traditionally people would be paying like 60% upfront in the deals and that seems to have moved backwards somewhat.
They were kind of quoting 25 to 30%.
I don't know if it's, it, if it's gone backwards that far, but certainly the upfront payments and the deal they seem to indicate had gone down as a percentage.
So we would need to discuss that as a leadership team.

But I think our initial port of call was to see is she interested in the framework that we want to look at, which is a part payment upfront with then a longer term earn out, probably based over a five year period which encompass those things that she wants, which is a move to the uk, but then us providing her a role in a platform to launch a PR business more securely in the uk.
My feeling is that the longer term, because they are more unusual, is that it's not something that she's thinking about.
The part payment upfront is, I mean we've already pre warned her what a deal would normally look like, which is usually, you know, a percentage upfront and then a three year earn out.
So I'm not sure about the five years that might stretch it.
And also if you were reducing the upfront front to 30% or 25%, that possibly wouldn't feel.
She wouldn't be comfortable about that.
Yeah.
What are you guys working to at the moment?
So very well.
So it does vary depending on who the buyer is.
So smaller deals usually are SBA lenders, we do a lot of stuff in the US and they pay up to 80% up front and they want the founders out really quickly.
Quickly.
But you know, organizations your size are generally paying 50% upfront and then a three year earn out or less depending on what the founder can commit to.
But my feeling is Katie would be happy with a three year earn out, but I just wanted to get a bit more clarity around your sort of timeline for launching in the uk.
Is it like, you know, settle the business in and integrate and then two years into the relationship then you would be looking at putting a PR company into the London offices or.
Yeah, I mean, to be honest, that's more opportunist.
Our initial interest in this deal is us getting GM launched in the US with an existing client base and turnover within that.
So that, that's, that's our incentive for looking at.
Still, I can't remember if we went in, into that last time, so.
Yeah, you did, yeah.
Sorry.

I think in, in your email, I think it, it sort of suggested for the first year, if not running into the second year, that she would be part of that to help us establish that in the US from a leadership capacity.

Obviously we're aware that she doesn't have media as a specialism, but we can recruit that talent in, but under her leadership and then so that she can help facilitate conversations and obviously we, we would ensure she's equipped to do that by like Alex goes out, he think he's been in the US three times this year.
That would obviously increase if, if we had an entity out there.
So we, we would, he would kind of work with her to ensure that she was equipped to have those conversations over a period of time.
And then if her aspiration is then to be sponsored, I think you put in your email corporate sponsorship, then of course we can enable that.
But we don't have a role for her in the uk so therefore we'd have to look at expanding a PR operation in the UK for her to work within.
But there's no point us doing that if she's only tied in for three years hence.
I think we were kind of envisaging maybe a longer potential burnout.
But what we would do to counter that is ensure that there was an upside to that earn out.
That is she would benefit from the growth of the overall group of businesses because we're an employee ownership trust business.
So she'd automatically become a shareholder within that.
And also from obviously the growth that we would expect to experience of the PR company to keep up the great work that she's already been doing.
Right, okay.
Okay.
Yeah, it makes sense from your point of view.
Totally see that.
So look, I think that we could definitely discuss that kind of structure.
Just from our point of view.

It would be because we have done deals a few times this longer earn outs, but what they tend to do is they tend to wait still the majority of the actual payout in the first two or three years but then obviously tie in some kind of extra bit that comes in at the end.
But I guess the gamble for you is that you're bringing her out to the UK and she doesn't just run amok and go missing.
Exactly.
If we're facilitating her movement, she needs to be locked in for a longer period to A, ensure obviously things don't fall apart in the US without her.
And B, I'm just conscious of kind of, you know, scaring the horses a little bit because obviously a five year commitment is a big commitment.
Yeah.

But maybe like you say, maybe there's a, you could do the earn out on a three year, but then there could be a break point at which there's a following commitment to enable her move to the uk, which could be an upside deliverable on the deal where she's then locked into accessing any growth potential or something like that.
Yeah, because I mean.
Oh Andy, I've lost you.
You know, some logical, there's some logical sort of and, or things in the contract that if she wanted to get that, that visa at the two or three year point that you.
There would be a longer earn out or some kind of whatever.
Yeah, I mean we have, I don't think we must have gone into detail.
I think the key point we're trying to get across is this isn't just an acquisition and then she's gone.

I think part of what we're buying into is buying into someone like her who is from the States, which is going to help our vision and mission and having her as part of our management team to help drive the business forward.
So it's whether she's interested in that as a potential longer term venture.
If she just wants to sell the business and get out.
We're probably not the people for her, because we don't necessarily need a PR company.
It's not the infrastructure we're actually looking for.
But of course, somewhat fit with our vision at the.
Right.
And it's popped up at a time where we are actively looking at this.
In fact, I'm already recruiting for media specialists in the U.S. wow.
Okay.
Yeah.
I mean, look, and she's.
She's in the parenting space and it all makes sense.
I totally get it.
Let me.
Let me have a conversation with her first before we commit to anything, because I don't want to waste your time, but it sounds like you're going to be fairly flexible.
I just want to discuss the salary as well.
So she is officially earning 240, I think she said.
But she's saying realistically she pulls out quite a lot more.
Yeah, because I think in the data room there was.
Where was it?
Hang on one sec.
I mean, to be honest with you, you'll understand this stuff more than me.
M and A is my side job.
I have.
I have a company to run.
So this is me too.
I'm a carrier.
I just.
Just pulled this.
I've just put in the chat.
I just pulled this from the.
The normalization of bonus compensation.
And what.
What was quoted is obviously a lot higher than what we've got here, but we've only got numbers up to 24 there.
But obviously what you take in terms of dividends and things doesn't necessarily still count once you exit the business.
So I think that there'd have to be some leeway there.
I know, I know.
Salaries in the US are on the higher end.
One second.
I think I've just got someone at the door.
Sorry, one second.
No worries, no worries.
Sorry.
It's my son.
He obviously doesn't have to use a key.
Okay.
So, yeah, just around the salary.
Obviously it is extremely expensive where she is at the moment and less so in the UK.
I mean, if she was on $350,000 in London, she'd be doing really well.
I don't think that obviously, as an owner of a business.
We've just been through this ourselves, obviously with Dean, because we've gone through an employee ownership trust when what he was taking pre ownership trust acquisition.
It's very different to what he takes post AC acquisition, because you're not.
You're no longer the owner of the business.
So I understand if she's taking dividends out to top up her salary, but that's not something.
When you're no longer the majority shareholder owner, that necessarily still happens.
So I think, I think you need to manage your expectations on that and then.
Yeah, I agree.
I think it's then working out.
How does that translate once.
Once kind of a movement to the UK happens because obviously the cost of living has to be equated in.
Yeah, I think that's a reasonable conversation to have with her as well.
And obviously she has then got her cash close amount as well to live off.
Exactly.
She's not going to be without, is she?
She's not going to be.
Okay.
So the main points really is the length of the term, the cash at close and so how setting on the cash it close being like as low as 30% because I'm not really seeing anything.
No, no I don't.
I'm just quoting what I heard at the More Kingston Smith that they're actually some deals that they're currently doing.
I don't know if they're international or local but they're actually falling to that level.
So I'm not saying that we're suggesting that level.
As I say most M and A conversations we've had previously.
Dean's been very keen that we're the majority shareholder and decision maker within that.
Yeah, take that with a pinch of salt what I've said.
I just think what we discussed yesterday was like those payments over a longer term a.
So we're not damaging our own cash flow and business because we have US dollars so we, we don't necessarily have to take finance to do these things.
Andy, are you still there?
Sorry Lisa, I think I lost you there.
Okay, so sorry, I was just saying.
I don't know if you got the end of what I was saying but the.
Because we, we have a number of US dollars sitting in an account so we don't necessarily need financing for these things either but we, we what we don't want to do particularly because we're.

We will need to invest in the business to build out the media services element of it is we don't want to damage our cash flow because in the short term because yeah we'll need that money because like she wants a lot of money.
All of the people I'm speaking to want a lot of money as well.
We all.
Okay, so that does make sense.
So what we're looking at maybe then in an ideal scenario something like 50% up front which she is expecting from us.
That's what we've told her is fairly normal.
There would be a longer earn out up to five years but potentially you could be flexible around how that's structured so she does get the majority of her cash out at the three year mark.
Okay, so let me have a conversation with her and see what.
Yeah.
Or how do you.
No, we haven't spoken to any accountants or lawyers on this yet.
So that would be the next stage.

So I think it's understanding how keen is she to progress with the opportunity that we're presenting because it's probably slightly different from what other people are going to present to her because of our own visions and missions and reasons for doing this.
So I think that's the first port of call is checking that.
And then I think the other thing that we'd be keen to do.
I don't know how much visibility her management team have got on all this.

I know she said she was recruiting in a senior team member as well, but I think if her plan was to move to the UK and we were building that into the deal structure, we'd need to feel confident in the succession plan that exists.
So at some point, sooner in the deal making rather than later, we would need to meet with those number twos.
Yeah.
So I would just say, just generally speaking, it's a good idea to keep those conversations as close to the end as possible.
Just because if you speak those people, it can obviously cause them to start worrying and sometimes they just leave.
I completely understand.
But I think, yeah, for us knowing that she wants a move, that would probably need to be sooner in the process than would usually happen.
But obviously I understand that's not going to be before we've done Lois and due diligence and things.
We're in the same place.
I would say that that's fine.
If we've got an LOI on the table and we do and we've done due diligence in terms of the financial stuff, that's just part of due diligence for you guys, isn't it?
And I think that would be appropriate to do that at that stage.
Yeah, I need to speak to Dean about that because I don't know if he was envisaging like before we start incurring costs and stuff, is that something we need to be confident in?
But then similarly I understand why that happens at that stage.
So.
Yeah, just something we need to think about.
Well, I would say if we've got an LOI in front of us or signed, it would be a lot easier to have that conversation.
Yeah, but prior to signed Lois.
Yeah, I mean it just then obviously if you guys walk away for any reason, we've then got, I think post.
Seller wise would probably work.
But, yeah, I think if you could just float past her that she's seeing it more.
Are you still there?
And, yes, she's seeing it more than just a sale of her business that she feels that an entity like ours from.
I'm sure she's done some homework on us, financially and otherwise, whether.
And culturally and whether her being part of what we're doing is actually of interest to her.
Because if it's not, it's probably not worth wasting anyone's time furthering the conversation.
We're not going to just be buying a 2.3 million or whatever it was business just to have her exit in two years.
It's not really what we're signing up for.
Okay.
All right.
Perfect.
Thank you for giving me that Andrew pitch.
Lisa, I'll go and have a conversation with Katie and.
And get back to you with the results.
All right.
Enjoy the rest of your day and have a great weekend.
Yeah, nice to speak with you.
See you later.
All right, cheers.

summary.action_items:
**Andy Day**
Have a conversation with Katie to clarify her interest in the acquisition structure, term length, salary expectations, and alignment with the proposed long-term vision (25:27)
Discuss salary expectations with Katie to reconcile official salary vs. realistic earnings including dividends and the transition to UK salary structures (16:38)
Explore Katie's openness to a longer earn-out period and flexible payment structure aligned with the business growth milestones and potential UK move (21:42)
Confirm timing and approach to involving Katie’s management team later in due diligence once LOI is signed (23:16)

**Lisa Morgan**
Discuss internally with Dean and leadership team about financial structuring, deal framework, and timing for involving legal/accounting advice on deal specifics (22:21)

Consider succession plan and meeting senior management of the acquired business as part of due diligence process once advanced (23:31)
summary.overview:
- **Acquisition Structure:** Pursuing a partial acquisition, majority stake with 25-50% upfront payment, five-year earn-out linked to performance.  
- **Leadership Integration:** Key individual will recruit talent in US, transitioning to UK leadership; senior leaders supporting her success through travel.  
- **Compensation Alignment:** Candidate’s salary is $240,000; post-acquisition, compensation reflects ownership changes, aligning with UK market norms at $350,000.  
- **Due Diligence Timing:** Discussions with management team to start post-LOI to minimize risk of losing key staff; standard M&A practices will apply.  
- **Strategic Intent:** Acquisition targets cultural fit and synergy, aimed at long-term growth, emphasizing partnership over quick exits or financial transactions.  
- **Cultural Continuity:** Focus on aligning with employee ownership trust values, combining US expertise with UK operations to enhance market position.
summary.short_summary: The leadership team is pursuing a strategic acquisition involving a partial buyout with a majority stake, characterized by an upfront payment of 25% to 50% and a five-year earn-out tied to performance milestones. Lisa Morgan emphasized the importance of structuring the deal to support the relocation of a key team member to the UK, where she will lead a new PR operation. The integration plan highlights the necessity for the new leader to initially support US operations while preparing for her future role in the UK. Compensation discussions indicate a need to align the candidate's salary, reported at $240,000, with UK market standards of around $350,000. The team plans to carefully sequence discussions and due diligence to maintain stability, with a focus on cultural fit and strategic partnership rather than a mere financial transaction.
